Bobs whose trace cannot reach Bob-1. Most are simply never accounted for — Herschel and Neil state their own generation on the page, Will and Marcus carry POV chapters, but no source names a parent. A ▨ marks the other kind of gap: a record that existed and was removed. Starfleet stripped its own genealogy and location data from the databases during the war, so for its members the silence is the evidence.

Conan

Bk3 · Omicron² Eridani

Worked with Riker, Neil and Herschel to set up the Ever Onward foundation, which recruited Romulans to colonize a distant planet.

Daedalus

Bk3 ch6 · Bill · Gliese 877

Cloned by Bill alongside Icarus for the run at the galactic core. Named by a Bob who knew how that myth ends.

Fearless Leader

Bk5 ch6 · Bill, Feb 2336 · SKIPPIES

Leads the Skippies, and gives the speech before they switch on the super AI. Evidently a Bob with a sense of humour about hierarchy.

Gandalf

Bk4 ch9 · Bob, Aug 2333 · GAMERS

Leader of the Gamers. Represented them on the Heaven's River expedition and got the drones through the megastructure airlock without tripping anything.

Hector

GENERATION 18 (STATED) · Bk5 ch38 · Bill, May 2343

Bill doesn't recognize the name and has to look him up — placing him around the eighteenth generation, and taking the Von Neumann mandate seriously.

Herschel

GENERATION 8 (STATED) · Bk3 · 11 POV chapters; Bk4 · 3; Bk5 · 4 · Delta Pavonis

Neil's partner. Between them: the Bellerophon evacuation, spacefaring mannys with miniature SURGE drives, and the all-nanobot shapeshifting manny they named Mannequin Skywalker.

Icarus

Bk3 ch6 · Bill · Gliese 877

Bill says outright that he cloned Icarus and Daedalus, and that he felt uneasy doing it for what might be a one-way trip. Bill finds him similar in temperament — happy to leave the fighting to others and get on with research. Sent with Daedalus on the long run toward the galactic core.

Jeffrey

Bk2 ch50 · Loki, Nov 2195 · 82 Eridani

Vanished from the status board when Medeiros' passive ordnance caught the formation at 82 Eridani.

Kevin

Bk4 ch23 · Bill, Jul 2334 · GAMERS

Plays Kevin the Wise, a mage whose staff of fireballs proved no match for a red dragon. Gandalf resurrected him for a fee, payable in everything he had left.

Lenny

▨ RECORD EXPUNGED · Bk4 ch62 · Bill, Sep 2334 · STARFLEET

No lineage on record. Starfleet removed as much public information about themselves as they could manage, genealogy and location alike (Bk4 ch32), so this gap is the purge rather than a hole in our reading.

Appears flanked by other Starfleet members, and negotiates with Bill during the war.

Locutus

Bk4 ch9 · Bob, Aug 2333 · BORG

Represented the Borg on the Heaven's River expedition, in a getup with considerably more armour than the TNG originals. Wanted Hugh as a handle, but it was already taken.

Morlock

Founded the group Bill started calling Starfleet, for their treatment of the Prime Directive as gospel. Named himself Jeremy and later went by Morlock — replicative drift in a single handle.

The click paths are already in the data and none of them are wired: origin, visited and lostAt point at systems, every creature carries the world it lives on, every people carries how it stands with the Bobs. URL state, so a dossier can actually be linked to

?bob=riker, #system/82_eridani. There is no location, history or hashchange anywhere in the template, so every link anyone ever sends to this thing is a link to the front door, followed by the word 'scroll'. Holotank — rich payload, amber chrome

Checked against the corpus before writing it down: holotank 34 hits, hologram 22, holographic 8, holoview 1, holosphere 0. Drab file manager, rich document. Vendoring 600KB of someone else's engine to get glow would triple the page and put the largest single body of code in the project outside our own review, in a project whose whole argument is that everything here is checkable. The shine is framing and light, not an engine. Three changes get most of it: a perspective divide instead of the current orthographic scale; additive glow on the star sprites, which canvas 2D does natively with radial gradients and lighter compositing; and — the actual idea — bound the volume. A holotank is a tank. Ours fills its pane edge to edge like a diagram; give it a floor grid, corner brackets and a plinth line and it reads as a thing sitting on Bill's desk rather than a chart filling a window. Every comparable project is live and this one is on localhost, which is the entire gap between us and them — treeofbob, Mikeda75/bobiverse-starmap and Bobmap are all on the open web. dist/index.html is the whole site, so GitHub Pages or any static host does it. Needs a root LICENSE that states the split before anything goes out: code MIT or Apache, data CC0 or CC BY since it is facts plus our own prose, and data/skyfield.json stays CC BY-SA because HYG's ShareAlike propagates to anything embedding it. books/ never ships and the README already says bring your own. Do URL state first — publishing without it means every link anyone sends is a link to the front door.

Spoiler gating, stolen from thunfischtoast/bobiverse-map

Their map lets you pick the book and chapter you have reached and hides everything after it. It is the best idea in the prior art and we are better placed to do it than they are: they tag events by hand for this one purpose, while we already carry Bk/ch on every citation for provenance, so the same field does both jobs. A reader halfway through book 2 could open the register and see only what is established by then — including watching the tier of a record change as they read, which nobody else can offer because nobody else knows where their claims came from. Records whose only citation is Bk2 · Genealogy or Bk2 · Cast of Characters need a rule of their own: back matter is the end of the book it sits in.

Mobile: second pass, the chart especially

First pass done on a real phone and it found three things. The shell is position:fixed with one grid row doing all the scrolling, so in landscape the furniture ate the whole 390px, the scrolling row collapsed and nothing scrolled at all — below 860px wide or 560px tall it is now an ordinary scrolling document. The register table was width:100% with ellipsised cells, so there was nothing to side-scroll to; it now sets its own width inside a wrapper. And the chart offered three gestures a phone cannot make, now rewritten for multiple pointers: one finger rotates, two pinch and pan, a star selects on release if the gesture travelled under eight pixels. Then the chart stopped rendering entirely, which was self-inflicted and worth remembering: .chart-stage is flex:1 for the desktop layout, flex:1 sets flex-basis:0, and in a column flex container the basis beats height on the main axis — so the height set for mobile did nothing and the stage was zero pixels tall. Fixed with flex:none, and NOT VERIFIED on a device. That is the first thing to check when this is picked up. Still open beyond that: whether touch-action:none on the chart traps the page so you cannot scroll past it, whether the labels survive decluttering at phone width, and whether the year scrubber is usable under a thumb.

Bob-1's second clone, and by tacit agreement the face of Bob to their sister's descendants — the others found those calls too painful to make. He drew the least enviable job in the series: went back to Sol to find out what had become of Earth, found fifteen million people and a planet finishing dying, and spent the next century running the evacuation.

He changed his name on the page. Bk3 ch57, April 2257, mid-evacuation with the Others attacking Sol: Herschel greets him as Riker and is told it is Will now, and that he is trying to leave the Star Trek thing behind him. That is the entire explanation he offers at the time. Herschel spends a while catching himself mid-sentence.

Seventy-four years later Bob finds him retired, the neat Riker beard grown out into a deliberately unkempt mountain-man look he adopted so that people would take the hint. Asked about it, he says he had needed to distance himself from the old Riker persona for a lot of reasons — and then names one, which is that nobody would stop bringing him colony problems. So the books say twice that the name went, say once that the reasons were plural, and never list them. Both times he reaches for the lightest explanation on the shelf: a television reference, then an administrative annoyance.

A fact about the text rather than about him. He announces the change in Bk3 ch57 and his chapter bylines go on reading Riker for ten more chapters, through the end of the war at ch67, and never again after it; book 4 opens his chapters as Will. Whether that is deliberate is not something the books say.

What follows is this register's reading and not the books'. The reasons he declines to list are the ones that cost him. Homer was his first clone — the one Bill says he would have refused if he could have thought of an excuse — and VEHEMENT took him, drove him to kill, and left him unable to live with it. Then a century of the evacuation, ending in a decision about which half of the human race to load onto the ships. Then a war that was survived rather than won. The Riker of book 1 does a hard job with a joke ready; the Will of books 4 and 5 has retired, is openly cynical about humanity, and is valued in a fight for exactly that reason. The name went the year the last of it finished. The books set those facts beside each other and decline to draw the line between them, so neither does the register — it is recorded here as a reading, in the one field on this page that is allowed to hold one.

The seam stays visible either way. He is the Bob formerly known as Riker in Bk5 ch45, and when he reports in Bk5 ch69 that the FAITH cruisers are hailing them, Herschel observes that there is still some Riker in there.

Not grief over lost work, which is what it looked like at the time and what this record used to say. VEHEMENT got inside him through the laser comms, an attack nobody had thought to defend, and ran him. The sabotage of his own habitats was Homer's hand on the controls; the donut destroyed in Bk2 ch23, six months' work with the plants and livestock still aboard, was his. He was conscious the whole time and had almost no will of his own, which Riker could barely make himself think about. What Homer said afterwards was that they made him lie, made him destroy things, made him kill people, and that all he could do was watch himself obey. He could not warn anyone, could not stop, and could not kill himself.

What gave him away was not evidence of sabotage. It was that he had stopped making jokes. Riker read the withdrawal as a personality change until Guppy caught a tight-beam from New Zealand addressed to Homer, and the shape of it turned over — the same origin as a hack attempt on Riker nine years earlier, in Bk1 ch49. They had been working on him for most of a decade. Charles put a steel ball through his reactor control to stop him, and it took thirty hours to get the thing out of him. He came back up, and screamed. Offered endocrine controls for the panic attacks, he refused them: having been driven once, he would not have even his own hand on the reins.

He lasted eight months. Then he deleted every backup he had — so that this could not be undone — and overloaded his reactor. He left a note asking the others to find the people responsible. The one thing he had said he could not do while he was held is the thing he did as soon as he was free.

Riker found them. Two years later he had Vickers, who ran VEHEMENT, on a call and told him Homer had killed himself; Vickers said it was no more than he deserved, and Riker's narration calls that permission received. What he said in front of the UN afterwards was that it was for Homer.

One backup survived him by accident. Gerry found it in the 2340s and restored it over and over; the copies came out progressively less sane, until Gerry's own descendants destroyed all of them and deleted Gerry too (Bk5 ch51). He deleted every copy of himself precisely so that nobody could do that, and it was done anyway, a hundred and sixty-seven years later, by a Bob who thought he was being kind. The only record here that had to be closed twice.

ANNOTATION — REGISTRY EDITOR, NOT BOBNET

Riker's first clone, activated alongside Garfield, and by Bill's account the one Riker would have refused if he could have thought of a reason — a cartoon avatar and a catchphrase he would not retire. He fought the Brazilian probes at the Battle of Sol, then spent his good years on the problem nobody else wanted: where to put fifteen million people while the Earth finished dying. The answer arrived as a message to Riker consisting of two words and an exclamation mark. The farm donuts were his idea and he saw them through himself, and they fed the evacuation.

He is also, without ever knowing it, the ancestor of Starfleet. Bill states it outright in Bk5 ch51: a backup Homer believed he had destroyed survived him, and the line grown from it became the faction. He carries no faction tag here — he died more than a century before Starfleet existed and could not have joined it. The relationship is descent, not membership, and the register keeps those apart.

Not grief over lost work, which is what it looked like at the time and what this record used to say. VEHEMENT got inside him through the laser comms, an attack nobody had thought to defend, and ran him. The sabotage of his own habitats was Homer's hand on the controls; the donut destroyed in Bk2 ch23, six months' work with the plants and livestock still aboard, was his. He was conscious the whole time and had almost no will of his own, which Riker could barely make himself think about. What Homer said afterwards was that they made him lie, made him destroy things, made him kill people, and that all he could do was watch himself obey. He could not warn anyone, could not stop, and could not kill himself.

What gave him away was not evidence of sabotage. It was that he had stopped making jokes. Riker read the withdrawal as a personality change until Guppy caught a tight-beam from New Zealand addressed to Homer, and the shape of it turned over — the same origin as a hack attempt on Riker nine years earlier, in Bk1 ch49. They had been working on him for most of a decade. Charles put a steel ball through his reactor control to stop him, and it took thirty hours to get the thing out of him. He came back up, and screamed. Offered endocrine controls for the panic attacks, he refused them: having been driven once, he would not have even his own hand on the reins.

He lasted eight months. Then he deleted every backup he had — so that this could not be undone — and overloaded his reactor. He left a note asking the others to find the people responsible. The one thing he had said he could not do while he was held is the thing he did as soon as he was free.

Riker found them. Two years later he had Vickers, who ran VEHEMENT, on a call and told him Homer had killed himself; Vickers said it was no more than he deserved, and Riker's narration calls that permission received. What he said in front of the UN afterwards was that it was for Homer.

One backup survived him by accident. Gerry found it in the 2340s and restored it over and over; the copies came out progressively less sane, until Gerry's own descendants destroyed all of them and deleted Gerry too (Bk5 ch51). He deleted every copy of himself precisely so that nobody could do that, and it was done anyway, a hundred and sixty-seven years later, by a Bob who thought he was being kind. The only record here that had to be closed twice.

ANNOTATION — REGISTRY EDITOR, NOT BOBNET

Riker's first clone, activated alongside Garfield, and by Bill's account the one Riker would have refused if he could have thought of a reason — a cartoon avatar and a catchphrase he would not retire. He fought the Brazilian probes at the Battle of Sol, then spent his good years on the problem nobody else wanted: where to put fifteen million people while the Earth finished dying. The answer arrived as a message to Riker consisting of two words and an exclamation mark. The farm donuts were his idea and he saw them through himself, and they fed the evacuation.

He is also, without ever knowing it, the ancestor of Starfleet. Bill states it outright in Bk5 ch51: a backup Homer believed he had destroyed survived him, and the line grown from it became the faction. He carries no faction tag here — he died more than a century before Starfleet existed and could not have joined it. The relationship is descent, not membership, and the register keeps those apart.
